references.rationale: S1 reports 74% weekly use and S2 establishes the service-member population and self-report method. About 75% is a reasonable rounded paraphrase of this historical survey estimate. The clip is from 2022: do not interpret it as a newly measured 2026 rate or an exact census. Approximation is acceptable; retain survey limitations.

A1 documents adverse-effect reports. F1 and O1 establish that hidden ingredients could produce positive tests, but give no observed positive-test case attributable to a supplement. Possibility is not documentation of occurrence. The packet is insufficient for the conjunction, not a refutation of the real-world claim.

The FDA examples establish that some marketed weight-loss products contain undeclared drugs. They do not quantify the fraction among effective products. The probabilistic generalization is not established or contradicted by this packet. Score the factual interpretation only; rhetoric versus literal intent still needs human review.

W1 and W2 describe variable needs and sources of total water intake. They neither validate this specific plain-water starting-point formula nor explicitly refute it. Variation does not logically disprove a qualified heuristic. Missing support warrants insufficient rather than contradicted. The video graphic resolves the example as 160 lb and 80 oz.

B1 describes trained behavioral-health clinicians providing BBT-I, and B2 explains the treatment. Interpret can as availability through appropriately trained clinicians, not permission for every consultant regardless of training. No universal cure or guarantee is claimed.

R1 and R2 support changing schedules and shift work as contributors to insomnia. Deployment supplies context, not a unique risk multiplier. Can does not imply certainty. The on-screen list says IRREGULAR WORK SCHEDULE DURING DEPLOYMENT; the publisher caption incorrectly says regular.

note: Freeze precedes candidate generation; timestamp/hash are reproducibility checks, not tamper-proof attestation.
